newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-"Redfellas," a new U.S. crime import from Russia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-"Redfellas," a new U.S. crime import from Russia.

text.p: A pink neon sign welcomes you to Porky's, a strip joint in a Cuban neighbourhood near Miami's international airport. Inside, naked girls cavort for a crowd of leering businessmen and sheepish college students.

The bouncers are Russian and so is the owner, Ludwig Fainberg, nicknamed Tarzan because of his wild hair. In the backrooms, federal law enforcement agents say, Fainberg ran a criminal enterprise whose activities read like a Hollywood script.

His operations, an indictment alleges, ran the gamut from prostitution to cocaine smuggling, and his business associates included Colombian drug barons and hard-up Russian military officers. His most audacious scheme was to try to broker the purchase of a submarine from Russia for cocaine cartels to use to smuggle vast amounts of narcotics into the United States.

Russian-born Fainberg, who holds an Israeli passport, is in jail awaiting trial on the 30-count indictment. And law enforcement officials believe his operation is only the vanguard of a new wave of mobsters joining Miami's colourful criminal mosaic -- the Russian mafia, dubbed "Redfellas" by crime fighters.
Fainberg was arrested after a three-year undercover operation by Drug Enforcement Administraion (DEA) agents backed by the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI).
BIG DEALS IN LITTLE HAVANA

"The deals were done in Porky's, people were entertained there, that's where they took the visiting Russians. He felt very comfortable there," DEA spokeswoman Pam Brown said of Fainberg. "We had a wiretap on them for six months. They were very free with their conversations."
Fainberg had good connections with the Colombians and the Cuban American gangs who run cocaine distribution in south Florida, agents told Reuters.

According to the indictment, he organised shipments of cocaine from Ecuador to St. Petersburg, Russia, packed in iced shrimp. He also visited Russia several times to arrange deals and negotiated to buy bullet-proof limousines and helicopters for Colombians, including Mi8 helicopters.

He was cutting a deal with Russian military officers to buy a Tango-class submarine from a St. Petersburg naval base for a drug cartel but was arrested before it went through. The $5.5 million price tag included a Russian captain and crew.

"They had an ex-admiral ready to sail it," one agent said. "The cartels have so much money that $5.5 million is nothing to them. That kind of money is tempting for an ex-serviceman in the old Soviet Union."
Louis Terminello, Fainberg's business lawyer and longtime friend, said the case against him was a "bizarre fantasy."
"MORE HYPE THAN ANYTHING"

"It appears to me to be a lot more hype than anything else," the lawyer said, adding that authorities had little evidence against Fainberg other than a taped telephone conversation to justify a long and costly operation.
"Fainberg's the type of guy who talks too much. He likes to make himself out to be bigger than he is," Terminello said.

Law enforcement officials say they are alarmed by the rise of Russian organised crime groups in Florida. Crime fighters first noticed them among the immigrant communities in New York after the Soviet Union's collapse.
Now, like Al Capone in the 1930s, the Mafia in the 1940s and 1950s and the Colombian "cocaine cowboys" in the 1980s, they have been drawn to the Sunshine State.
"The Russian crime problem here is new and emerging. We don't have much intelligence on them yet," FBI agent Hardrick Crawford said. "We're still playing catch-up."
Although they are labeled Russians, the mobsters come from all parts of the former Soviet Union from Latvia to Kazakhstan, Crawford said.
The FBI opened an office in Moscow in 1994 to liase with Russian police and formed an anti-Russian crime unit in 1995.
BRUTAL, AND COMPUTER LITERATE
"The Russian mafias can be very brutal. They are very sophisticated. They are computer literate," Crawford said. "They hit the ground running.

They had linked up quickly with the Colombians, for whom Miami remains the cocaine trade's command and control centre for drug smuggling. Money-laundering and fraud, prostitution and protection rackets were also on their list of interests.
Agents believe Russian girls are lured here under false pretences and forced to work in the sex trade with threats of violence.

Florida was ideal for the Russian gangs, Crawford said, and not just because of the weather. It is a boom town, the gateway to Latin America and a place where crime groups operate alongside one other rather than fighting each other.

The task of law officers was made harder because Russian, unlike Spanish, was an alien language in south Florida. More officers and agents with language skills were being brought in, Crawford said, adding "We are in it for the long haul."
Meanwhile, at Porky's, the Russian girls have left the stage since Fainberg's arrest. "Maybe they weren't earning enough money," one employee suggested by way of explanation.
